Employment Scams UK: Fake Jobs, Fees & Mule Recruitment

Fake recruiters on LinkedIn and Indeed, up-front fees, bounced cheques and reshipping work. What UK agencies may charge, and how to check an offer.

A job scam does not need a convincing company — it needs a convincing reason to move fast. The offer arrives without an interview, or after one held entirely over chat, and the first real request is money, documents or your bank details.

One rule settles most of it: in Great Britain, employment agencies and businesses may not charge you a fee for finding you work. If a ‘recruiter’ wants payment for training, equipment, a DBS check or a placement, that is the end of the conversation.

Where the approach comes from

Most begin on a platform you already trust. Our LinkedIn job scam guide covers recruiter impersonation, and our Indeed job scam guide covers listings posted under a real employer’s name. A cold ‘you’re hired’ message with no application behind it is the simplest version of all.

Agencies themselves are impersonated too — our recruitment agency scam guide covers how to check one is real before sending documents.

The four shapes the money takes

An up-front fee for training, kit, a uniform or a background check. A cheque that clears and then bounces, after you have forwarded part of it — the mystery shopper scam runs on exactly this. Equipment you pay for and never receive, common in data entry job offers and other remote work listings. Your account used to move someone else’s money, which is money mule recruitment.

Our work from home scam guide covers envelope-stuffing, kit fees and reshipping, where parcels bought with stolen cards are posted on from your address.

What a UK employer or agency may actually ask for

An employer may ask for right-to-work documents and bank details once an offer is real and you have met or spoken to them properly. A criminal record check is requested through DBS in England and Wales, Disclosure Scotland, or AccessNI — and the employer arranges it rather than asking you to pay a ‘recruiter’ for one.

Under the Conduct of Employment Agencies and Employment Businesses Regulations 2003, work-finding services cannot charge a jobseeker a fee, with narrow exceptions set out in Schedule 3 — specified performers and creative occupations, photographic and fashion models, and professional sports people. Great Britain and Northern Ireland have separate regulations.

How to check an offer before you send anything

Find the company yourself rather than using contact details in the message, and call the switchboard listed on its own site to confirm the role and the recruiter’s name. Check the recruiter’s profile history rather than the profile alone — a brand-new account with a stock photo is worth pausing over.

Ask for the offer in writing, and read where it says payment is expected from you. Do not accept money into your account to pass on, whatever the explanation.

If you have paid or shared details

Tell your bank immediately and say the payment may be authorised push payment fraud. If you sent identity documents, consider Cifas Protective Registration, which flags your details for extra checks before credit is granted in your name.

Check your credit report for applications you did not make — MoneyHelper lists the agencies offering a free statutory report.

If your account was used to receive and forward money, tell your bank even so; that conversation is far better had early.

How to report a job scam in the UK

Report the listing or profile on the platform, then report the fraud to Report Fraud at reportfraud.police.uk or 0300 123 2040 in England, Wales and Northern Ireland, or Police Scotland on 101 in Scotland.

Problems with a named employment agency can also go to the Employment Agency Standards Inspectorate through GOV.UK. Forward scam texts free to 7726 and suspicious emails to report@phishing.gov.uk.

Common questions

Can a UK recruitment agency charge me to find work?

No, for work-finding services. The Conduct of Employment Agencies and Employment Businesses Regulations 2003 prohibit charging a jobseeker a fee to find them work, with narrow Schedule 3 exceptions covering specified performers and creative occupations, photographic and fashion models, and professional sports people. Great Britain and Northern Ireland have separate regulations.

The cheque cleared, so the job must be real?

Not necessarily. Funds appearing in your account is not the same as a cheque having cleared for good. A cheque can be returned unpaid weeks later, and anything you forwarded in the meantime comes out of your own money.

Is it illegal to receive money into my account for an employer?

It can make you a money mule, which is a criminal offence even where you believed the job was genuine. Legitimate employers pay you; they do not route other people's money through your account.

What should I do if I sent copies of my passport or driving licence?

Consider Cifas Protective Registration so lenders carry out extra checks in your name, and monitor your credit report. Report it to Report Fraud, or Police Scotland on 101 in Scotland.
